I am sixty-nine years old and have worked this land in Quzhou County for forty-seven years. I never went to school, but the land has been my teacher. It is just my husband and me now — two mouths, two pairs of hands — and our seven mu of well-irrigated land. We have always done wheat-maize double cropping, and I see no reason to change what has fed us for so long.

For **wheat**, I will rotary-till the fields after the autumn corn stubble is cleared and sow around early October. I use our local improved wheat seed at about thirty-five jin per mu — not the old traditional seeds, but not fancy either, just the kind that has done well here for years. I spread one hundred jin of compound fertilizer per mu as basal dressing, and when the wheat greens up in spring I topdress with eighty jin of urea. I will irrigate twice from our well: once after sowing if the soil is dry, and once at jointing when the wheat needs it most. I spray five times in total — twice for insects, once for weeds, and twice for fungus when the weather turns damp. I know my land well enough to expect around one thousand one hundred jin per mu if the winter is not too cruel.

For **maize**, I sow denghai605 hybrid seed right after wheat harvest in early June — about one package and a bit per mu. There is no time to plough between crops, so I plant without tillage; the stubble mulch keeps moisture in and saves diesel. I put down one hundred jin of compound fertilizer per mu at sowing. I irrigate twice in the summer when the well water is needed most, and I spray five times for pests, weeds, and the leaf diseases that come with the summer heat. I expect about nine hundred thirty-five jin per mu — not the highest in the village, but steady.

I do not experiment. I have seen too many neighbors lose money chasing new varieties or cutting fertilizer to save a few yuan. My way works.
